opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is to stop treating them as competitors. People sometimes frame it as "classical simulation versus learned simulation," as if one will replace the other. I don't think that's the right picture. Each side has strengths the other lacks, and the interesting work is in combining them carefully.

Physical simulators encode decades of understanding: conservation laws, contact, elasticity, fluid dynamics. That structure is valuable. It gives you generalization for free in a way that's very hard for a purely data-driven model to match. If you train a network on a thousand videos of a cube falling, it may or may not handle a slightly different shape or mass. A good simulator just does, because the physics is the physics.

But simulators have real weaknesses for robotics. The first is the sim-to-real gap. Real materials, friction, and actuators are messy, and our models of them are approximations. The second is that traditional simulators are often black boxes from an optimization point of view. You run them forward and get a result, but you can't easily ask, "How should I change the controller, or the material parameters, to get a better outcome?"

That's where I think the connection to neural networks becomes very natural. One direction I care a lot about is differentiable simulation. If the simulator is differentiable, it becomes just another layer in your computational graph. You can backpropagate through the physics, into a neural network controller, or into the physical parameters themselves. That lets you do things like:

- **Optimize controllers with gradients** instead of relying only on reinforcement learning's trial and error, which can be dramatically more sample-efficient for some tasks.
- **Do system identification.** Take real-world observations and fit the simulator's parameters so the simulation actually matches reality. That directly attacks the sim-to-real problem.
- **Co-design.** Jointly optimize a robot's body and its controller, which is very hard without gradients.

There are caveats. Gradients through contact and discontinuities can be noisy or misleading, and long time horizons can lead to exploding or vanishing gradients. So differentiability isn't magic. You need to think about the numerical methods and sometimes combine gradient-based and sampling-based approaches.

The other direction is using neural networks *inside* the simulator, for the parts we can't model well from first principles. Keep the rigid-body or continuum mechanics core, but let a learned component model complicated friction, a residual correction, or a hard-to-characterize material. That hybrid approach tends to work better than either extreme. You keep the inductive bias of physics and let the data fill in what the equations miss.

And there's a very practical, systems side that I think people underestimate: performance and usability. For robotics, you need simulation that's fast, massively parallel on GPUs, and easy enough to modify that researchers actually experiment with it. A lot of my motivation in building programming tools for simulation came from that. If writing a new, high-performance, differentiable simulator takes months of CUDA engineering, very few people will do it. If it takes days, the whole field moves faster.

So my short answer: use physics as the backbone, make it differentiable and fast, and use neural networks to close the gap with reality and to act as the controllers and policies on top. The magic happens in the interface between the two.

r001.rationale: The response attributes simulation error to approximate models of messy materials, friction, and actuators, while describing the underlying physics as valid.

r002.rationale: It proposes learned simulator components and residual corrections to address what physical equations miss and help close the sim-to-real gap.

r003.rationale: It discusses the inductive bias of physical simulators, but does not observe that nominally end-to-end neural networks still incorporate inductive biases.

r004.rationale: It mentions sample efficiency and the need for fast simulation, but does not connect practical compute and data limits to incorporating physical-world inductive biases into neural networks.

r005.rationale: It cautions about noisy gradients and numerical issues, but not that imposing too much prior structure can underestimate a model’s learning capacity.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that neither side wins on its own, and the interesting work is in the seams between them.

Pure physics simulation gives you something neural networks still struggle with: generalization you can actually reason about. If I write down the equations for an elastic body or a granular material and solve them properly, the simulator behaves correctly in situations nobody put in a training set. That matters enormously for robotics, because the whole point of a simulator is to prepare a robot for things it hasn't seen yet. But classical simulators have real limits. They're expensive, they're often hard to differentiate through, and there's always a gap between the idealized model and the messy object sitting on the table. Friction, contact, deformable stuff, fluids, those are places where our equations are approximations and our parameters are guesses.

Neural networks are good at exactly the things physics is bad at. They can absorb data from the real world and close that gap. They can learn a constitutive model for a material you don't have a clean analytic description for. They can act as fast surrogates when you need thousands of rollouts per second for planning or reinforcement learning. So the question isn't physics versus learning. It's where in the pipeline you put the learned component so you keep the structure that physics gives you.

My view, which comes a lot from the work on differentiable simulation, is that the simulator itself should be a first-class citizen in the learning loop. If your simulator is differentiable, it stops being just a data generator and becomes part of the model. You can backpropagate through contact and material dynamics to fit parameters from a handful of real observations. You can train a policy with gradients from the physics instead of relying only on noisy reward signals. And you can plug a network into the middle of the simulator, say for the parts of the dynamics you don't trust, while the rest stays grounded in conservation laws. That hybrid tends to be far more data efficient and far more trustworthy than a network trained end to end to imitate a whole world.

There's also a very practical infrastructure problem underneath all this, and it's one I care about a lot. Physical simulation and deep learning have historically lived in different software ecosystems with different performance characteristics. Simulation code is sparse, irregular, and full of spatial data structures. Deep learning frameworks are built around dense tensors. If you want these two things to work together, you need tools that let a researcher write a high-performance simulator in a few hundred lines and have it compose cleanly with gradient-based training. A lot of the reason people reach for purely learned simulators is just that writing a real one was too painful. Lower that barrier, and the hybrid approach becomes the natural default rather than the heroic exception.

So if I had to summarize: use physics for structure and extrapolation, use learning to absorb reality and buy speed, make the whole thing differentiable so the two can actually talk to each other, and invest in the programming systems that make that combination easy to build. That's how I think simulators go from being a nice-to-have for robotics to something robots genuinely learn from.

r001.rationale: The response says physical models can be approximations with guessed parameters, but does not clearly distinguish those modeling errors from errors in fundamental laws.

r002.rationale: It proposes using learned components to absorb real-world data and close the gap between idealized simulation and reality.

r003.rationale: It discusses physics-based structure and end-to-end imitation, but does not observe that end-to-end neural networks still have inductive biases.

r004.rationale: It notes that simulation can be expensive and that hybrid approaches can be data-efficient, but does not clearly connect compute and data limits to adding physical-world inductive biases to neural networks.

r005.rationale: It does not caution that imposing too much prior structure could limit or underestimate a model’s learning capacity.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re very complementary. Physical simulation gives us a structured way to predict what happens when a robot takes an action. But a simulator is always an approximation. Contact, friction, soft materials—these are difficult to model perfectly, and often we don’t even know the right parameters.

Neural networks can help fill those gaps. Rather than asking a network to learn all of physics from scratch, we can use the simulator for the parts we understand and learn the parts we don’t understand well from real-world data. The important thing is that this combination predicts the consequences of the robot’s actions more accurately.

Differentiable simulation is also useful here. If you can compute how an outcome changes when you change a physical parameter or a control input, you can use that information to fit the simulator to observations or improve a controller. That creates a tighter loop between learning and simulation.

For robotics, I think the goal should be a simulator that gets better as the robot gathers experience. You collect data, improve the model, train the policy, and then test it in the real world. It doesn’t have to reproduce every detail of reality, but it needs to capture the details that matter for the task.

r001.rationale: It attributes simulation error to approximations in modeling contact, friction, and soft materials, and to uncertain parameters.

r002.rationale: It proposes learning poorly modeled parts from real-world data to improve predictions and the simulator.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss inductive biases in nominally end-to-end neural networks.

r004.rationale: It does not connect compute or data limits to incorporating physical-world inductive biases into neural networks.

r005.rationale: It does not caution that excessive prior structure can limit a model’s capacity to learn.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most useful approach is to combine the strengths of both. With physical simulation, we already know quite a lot about how the world works. We have equations for motion, contact, and deformation. But when you put a robot in the real world, there are always things you don’t know precisely: friction, material properties, or how an object will respond when you touch it.

Neural networks can help us learn those missing pieces from data. Instead of asking a network to learn all of physics from scratch, we can build a simulator around physical principles and learn the parts that are difficult to model.

Differentiable simulation is an interesting connection here. If you can compute how a robot’s behavior changes when you change a parameter, you can use that information to identify physical properties or improve a controller. You run an experiment, compare the simulation with what actually happened, and adjust the model.

For robotics, the goal is to make simulation useful for making decisions in the real world. So I would like to see a loop where the robot collects data, the simulator becomes more accurate, and that improved simulator helps the robot learn better behavior.

r001.rationale: It says the equations for motion, contact, and deformation are known, while friction, material properties, and object response are uncertain modeling details.

r002.rationale: It proposes learning the difficult-to-model parts from data and comparing simulation with real outcomes to adjust the model.

r003.rationale: It does not mention inductive biases in end-to-end neural networks.

r004.rationale: It gives no compute or data limits as a reason to build physical-world biases into neural networks.

r005.rationale: It does not caution that too much prior structure could limit a model’s learning capacity.
